title: VQActFlow: Action Mode Steering
description: Vector-quantized action generation for multi-task robot manipulation that steers which task a policy commits to at inference time, validated on a Unitree G1 humanoid, a bimanual platform, and LIBERO in simulation.

sections.content: In multi-task manipulation, a policy has to commit to the action mode that matches the current instruction. Pick the wrong mode and the robot does the wrong task. VQActFlow tokenizes action chunks into a discrete codebook and generates the codes with Variational Flow Matching, so it carries a distribution over action modes through every step of generation. At inference time, classifier-free guidance and a learned codebook critic reshape that distribution, and neither one retrains the policy.

sections.heading: Results
bullets: 81.0% peak success on LIBERO-Goal (w=4), vs. 61.5% for the closest discrete baseline.
80.5% success on LIBERO-90 with CFG and the codebook critic, the best of every baseline run.
57.5% success on Unitree G1 humanoid hardware at w=6, up from 23.8% with no guidance.
77.5% average success on an ALOHA-style bimanual platform with CFG and the critic together.

sections.heading: Key Contributions
bullets: Designed a VQ-VAE action tokenizer that compresses action chunks into a discrete codebook of reusable motion primitives.
Trained a Variational Flow Matching generator over codebook indices, preserving a full distribution over action modes during generation.
Developed inference-time steering with classifier-free guidance and a learned codebook critic, with no policy retraining required.
Validated on real hardware: Unitree G1 humanoid and ALOHA-style bimanual manipulation, plus LIBERO benchmarks in simulation.

sections.heading: Publication
sections.content: Zhigen Zhao, Mark Leggiero, Yipu Chen, Haoran Liu, Yifan Wu, Huishu Xue, Sirui Zhan, Ye Zhao, "VQActFlow: Vector-Quantized Action Mode Steering for Multi-Task Robot Manipulation," arXiv:2606.21600 (2026). Second of eight authors.

title: burg-bot: Autonomous Mapping Robot
description: A differential-drive robot running ROS 2 Jazzy that maps a space on its own, with no joystick and no waypoints, while a 7-inch display gives it a face that reacts to what it is actually doing.

sections.content: burg-bot is a TurtleBot3-Burger-style differential-drive robot running ROS 2 Jazzy on a Raspberry Pi 4, with a full autonomy stack, an expressive animated face, and camera-based semantic mapping. It maps a space on its own, with no joystick and no waypoints, while a 7-inch display gives it a face that reacts to what it is actually doing, and a depth camera labels the objects it finds and pins them to the map.

sections.heading: Autonomous Mapping
sections.content: A frontier is the boundary between explored free space and the unknown, and driving to one is the entire idea behind autonomous exploration. The exploration package finds those boundaries, scores each by size and distance, and sends the winner to Nav2. It stops when no frontier remains, which is also what guarantees no unexplored pockets are left behind.
bullets: Frontier detection and scoring are pure functions over an occupancy grid: plain arrays in, plain dataclasses out. The node is a thin wrapper that reads the map, calls into that module, and dispatches goals.
That split means the algorithm is unit-tested on small synthetic grids with no ROS graph, map server or SLAM running. The expression arbiter and the gesture library follow the same pattern.
Frontier cells are found with 8-connectivity rather than 4, so a boundary that only touches unknown space diagonally still counts. That happens constantly along a coarsely-resolved edge.
Each goal targets the cluster's nearest frontier cell to its own centroid, not the centroid itself, which can land off the frontier entirely for a concave or banana-shaped cluster.
Nav2 handles planning and control, robot_localization fuses wheel odometry with the IMU through an EKF, and slam_toolbox builds the map.

sections.heading: Expression as Telemetry
sections.content: Nothing the face does is decorative. Every mood traces back to something true about the robot: navigation status, lidar proximity, pose covariance, battery level, touch. If the eyes look uncertain it is because the localization covariance genuinely grew, and if they look tired the battery genuinely is. That makes the face a piece of honest telemetry you can read across a room, which is far more useful than a mood that is merely charming.
bullets: Half a dozen independent sources have an opinion about the face at once. Publishing them all straight to the renderer makes it flicker between them, and a flickering face does not read as conflicted; it reads as broken.
So each source submits a candidate with a priority and an expiry, and exactly one wins. That is the same shape as twist_mux arbitrating velocity commands, applied to expression.

Four priority bands: ambient personality is the floor and is always present, current task sits above it, recoverable trouble above that, and immediate physical events always show. That last band covers a lidar return inside 22 cm, the safety stop firing, or someone touching the screen.
A minimum hold stops two equal-priority sources swapping the face every tick, while a genuine escalation still preempts instantly.
The arbiter is pure logic with no ROS dependency, so it can be reasoned about and unit-tested without a graph running.

sections.heading: Semantic Mapping
sections.content: A YOLOv8n detector runs on the colour stream. Detections are back-projected to 3D using the aligned depth image and a pinhole model, transformed into the map frame, and folded into a persistent de-duplicated object layer that saves alongside the SLAM map.
bullets: The object layer is deliberately parallel to the occupancy grid rather than part of it, because a probability grid is not a place to store "this cell is a chair".
Inference is throttled to roughly 1.5 Hz rather than run per frame. The Pi 4 has no GPU or NPU, and objects worth labelling on a map do not move fast.

In the Gazebo testbed the chair was recognised at 0.88–0.95 confidence and tracked to within about 0.2 m of its true placement from 9 observations. That offset is expected rather than error: depth is sampled at the bounding-box centre, so the point lands on whichever surface faces the robot, not the object's centroid.

sections.heading: Hardware
bullets: Raspberry Pi 4 (4 GB) running Ubuntu 24.04 Server as the main compute.
Raspberry Pi Pico handling motor control and encoders over serial, behind a ros2_control hardware interface.
DC motors with encoders for differential drive, a 2D lidar for SLAM and obstacle avoidance, and an MPU6050 IMU fused with wheel odometry via EKF.

The official Raspberry Pi 7-inch touch display for the face, over DSI. SDL renders straight to the panel through KMS/DRM, with no X, no Wayland and no desktop session, which is why the robot can run Ubuntu Server and still have a face.
Intel RealSense D435 for object detection and 3D projection.
Everything builds and runs in a container, so the Ubuntu 24.04 / ROS 2 Jazzy target need not match the development host.

sections.heading: Credit
sections.content: The physical robot design and the foundational ROS 2 packages come from Antonio Brandi's course, Self-Driving and ROS 2 - Learn by Doing! Plan & Navigation. The description, controller, firmware, localization, mapping, navigation and safety-stop packages derive from that work. Original to this repository are the procedural face renderer, the mood arbiter and gesture library, frontier-based exploration, the perception and semantic-mapping stack, the custom message interfaces, the Docker development environment and the Gazebo testbed.

title: Mimic: 3-Axis Robot Arm
description: A 3-axis brushless DC robot arm using ODrive motor controllers, custom KiCAD PCB design, and CAN bus communication, built to learn industrial motion control.

sections.content: Mimic is a personal project to design and build a capable robot arm using industrial-grade components rather than hobby servos. The goal is to learn brushless motor control, power electronics, encoder feedback, and real-time communication protocols used in professional robotic systems.

sections.heading: System Architecture
bullets: 3 axes driven by EaglePro 8803 BLDC motors with ODrive S1 motor controllers for FOC (Field-Oriented Control).
AS5600 magnetic encoders for precise angular position feedback on each joint.
120VAC to 24VDC power supply with 24V-to-12V buck converter for logic power, and 24V relay-based motor enable circuit with hardware e-stop.
USB-C to CAN adapter for real-time host communication over CAN bus.
Custom KiCAD schematic and PCB design for clean wiring and brake resistor integration.

sections.heading: Key Contributions
bullets: Designed full electrical schematic in KiCAD including power distribution, motor drives, encoder interfaces, and safety circuits.
Integrated brake resistors for regenerative braking energy dissipation on each ODrive channel.
Built custom 3D-printed structural components for the arm links and joints.
Developing Python control software for trajectory planning and teleoperation.

title: MacGyver Bot: Self-Balancing Robot
role: Personal Project, Built in Rural Kenya
description: A PID-controlled two-wheeled self-balancing robot built using only materials accessible in a rural Kenyan village.

sections.content: Two-wheeled self-balancing robot built using only parts available from Kenyan companies serving rural villages: hobby-grade geared motors, 18650 lipo batteries, an H-bridge motor controller, and an ESP32 microcontroller.

sections.heading: Key Contributions
bullets: Used Kalman filtering to improve the signal of the low-cost MPU6050 gyroscope for accurate angle measurement.
Implemented PID controller for motor control to provide stability.
Currently sourcing motor encoders to enhance stability and transitioning to microROS for external computer communication.

gallery.caption: Tilt angle over time while balancing, logged from the ESP32. The excursions are the disturbances it recovers from.

title: Micro-Spot Quadruped Robot
description: A fully 3D-printed 12-DoF quadruped robot with custom inverse kinematics, controlled via ROS2 and Raspberry Pi.

sections.content: Fully 3D-printed quadruped in development using 12 servo actuators and ESP32 microcontroller. Personally developed inverse kinematic code and algorithm for limb movements given desired end-effector position.

sections.heading: Key Contributions
bullets: Learned inverse kinematic techniques to control basic coordinated limb movements: standing, sitting, pan, tilt, and roll.
Created an iterative algorithm for solving servo angles for correct end-effector spatial placement with minimal travel distance.
Wrote end-effector optimal movement software in Python for use as a ROS2 service.
Currently researching quadruped gait for walking using reinforcement learning on a Raspberry Pi 4, and redesigning leg limbs for more natural movements.

gallery.caption: Stepping through its gait on a glass table, tethered to the laptop running the controller.
Body-roll demo: the feet hold their stance while the body rotates, which is the inverse-kinematics solver holding foot positions fixed in the world frame.
The build on the bench: twelve servos, a printed frame, and the wiring harness before the covers went on.
Limb-movement model: the commanded foot trajectories for one gait cycle, plotted in the body frame.

title: SMART Sea Level Sensors
description: Incorporated rainfall sensors into an IoT mesh network of water-level sensors used by climate researchers and disaster relief managers in Chatham County, Georgia.

sections.heading: The Problem
sections.content: The Smart Sea Level Sensors project operates a mesh network of water-level sensors in Chatham county, Georgia, used by climate researchers and disaster relief managers. To provide more comprehensive environmental data, rainfall sensors needed to be incorporated into the network.

sections.heading: The Solution
sections.content: Add high-grade rainfall sensors using the existing LoRaWAN IoT network hardware, and ensure the system is battery powered, running for at least 6 months without replacement. This greatly improves the ability of county management to monitor and predict heavy storms and floods.

sections.heading: Key Contributions
bullets: Conducted market analysis for optimal rain gauge sensor given price, power requirements, accuracy, and measurement resolution, and selected the TB4 tipping-bucket rain gauge.
Developed a low-power algorithm that records rainfall on triggered interrupt events using C/C++ on the GaTech Environmental Sensor ESP-32 development board.
Used LoRaWAN small packet communication to relay data to an IoT server.
Currently 12+ rain gauges are sending continuous rainfall measurements to the SMART Sea Level Sensors dashboard.

gallery.caption: A deployed node on a dock piling: the sea level sensor below and the rain gauge above, on the same enclosure.
Control flow for the rain gauge: bucket tips wake the ultra-low-power coprocessor, temperature and pressure are sampled every five minutes, and readings go out over the gateway to the API dashboard.

title: ERNEST: Sample Exchange Robot
description: Developed a highly precise robotic sample exchange system using a 3-axis piezo-electric manipulator for the Hard X-Ray Nanoprobe at Brookhaven National Laboratory.

sections.heading: The Problem
sections.content: The sample exchange process at the Hard X-Ray Nanoprobe (HXN) beamline at the National Synchrotron Light Source-II (NSLS-II) in Brookhaven National Laboratory requires breaking the vacuum with subsequent thermalization of the microscope's components which may take up to a few hours.

sections.heading: The Solution
sections.content: To increase efficiency and throughput of the HXN end station, develop an internal automatic sample exchange system, the Exchange Robot for the Nanoprobe Experimental Station (ERNEST), that enables a quick and reliable sample exchange process.

sections.heading: Key Contributions
bullets: Performed system calibration for strain gauges and linear encoders for all axes with high-accuracy calibration and position repeatability testing.
Created animation to preview movements using Fusion360 simulation.
Designed the sample pegs and environment for manufacturing in the lab machine shop.
Wrote the control algorithm in LabVIEW with accompanying GUI. The piezo-electric linear actuators achieved less than 10 nanometer precision in all movements.
Used force-sensing and placement for all actions to confirm positions.
Selected to give a poster presentation and oral presentation to laboratory staff.

gallery.caption: CAD animation of the sample-exchange assembly: the vertical actuator stack travelling over the linear stage that carries the sample rail.
Position sensing at 9× speed. Before any exchange, the end-effector sweeps to find the stage, since the routine cannot trust an assumed origin.
Sample exchange, grabbing, at 2× speed: the jaws close on one pin out of the seven-slot rail and lift it clear.
Sample exchange, loading, at 2× speed. The pin is seated with a controlled downward force rather than dropped, which is what keeps placement repeatable.

title: VAMPIRE: Fast Radiative Heat Analysis
role: Student Researcher, Vogel Lab, University of North Georgia
description: Developed an end-to-end method for estimating the radiative heat loss from structures in the built-environment using drone-based thermal imaging.

sections.heading: The Problem
sections.content: There are limited ways to estimate the radiative heat loss from a building's surface (envelope). With the growing threat of climate change pushing for more sophisticated ways of improving energy efficiency in buildings, I collaborated with two research professors and other students to design an end-to-end workflow for obtaining the total radiative heat loss from a structure.

sections.heading: The Solution
sections.content: Our method, dubbed VAMPIRE, uses drones outfitted with thermal cameras, surface-from-motion photogrammetry, and numerical surface integration software I designed to process thermal OBJ files.

sections.heading: Key Contributions
bullets: Researched flight paths, view angles, and image overlap for optimal thermographic 3D model creation using DJI Inspire 1 drone with Zenmuse XT 1 thermal imager.
Used Agisoft Metashape photogrammetry software to generate 3D thermal models from thermal images and tagged drone positions.
Created software to discretize building thermal models and perform surface numerical integration through the OBJ file structure.
Developed a GUI in MATLAB to streamline processing of thermal OBJ files.
Published as primary author in the journal Energy and Buildings.

sections.heading: Publication
sections.content: Mark Leggiero, Bradley Andrew, Ryan Elliott, John Indergaard, J.B. Sharma, Thomas Vogel, "Radiative heat loss estimation of building envelopes based on 3D thermographic models utilizing small unmanned aerial systems (sUAS)", Energy and Buildings, Volume 244, 2021.

gallery.caption: Three flight paths trialled for thermographic capture: (a) a rectangular grid at constant altitude and 90° view angle, (b) a single-altitude circular path at roughly 45°, and (c) the most effective — an ascending multi-circular path conforming to the building geometry, at view angles below 45°.
The 3D thermographic model creation process in Agisoft Metashape: point cloud from photogrammetry (left), triangular mesh built from it (middle), and the thermal texture mapped on top (right).
Rogers Hall as a thermographic model. The post-processed version (bottom right) has surrounding buildings, trees, and the roof removed, since they do not contribute to the envelope analysis.
The VAMPIRE Tools algorithm: how an OBJ file is restructured so that area, average temperature, and ground angle can be computed per mesh face, then integrated into a power output.
The MATLAB interface I built for the automated analysis — OBJ and texture in, ambient and dew point conditions set, radiative power out for three models.

A thermal image of one side of the Nesbitt building in FLIR Tools, with area measurements for brick siding and window. Enough such measurements estimate the loss by hand, which is what the automated result was checked against.
Verification against a known 9-W source: the texture file holding all thermal overlay data for the ‘unfolded’ box model, beside the box itself in Blender.
The Nesbitt building model, before and after removing surrounding structures, trees, and surfaces outside the envelope analysis.

title: Keep The Beep
description: Designed a ruggedized soft housing for GE Carescape physiological monitors to prevent damage during high-pressure patient transport.

sections.heading: The Problem
sections.content: Emory University Hospital relies on the GE Carescape B450 physiological monitor, however it is frequently damaged during high-pressure patient transport due to rough handling and loose mounting on hospital beds.

sections.heading: The Solution
sections.content: Create a soft protective housing designed for manufacture and tested for use in Emory Hospital Midtown. The case must protect all monitor regions from impact, be chemically inert, and easily sanitized.

sections.heading: Key Contributions
bullets: Used FaroArm Quantum 3D Scanner and 3D printing to enable rapid design and prototyping, quickly importing geometry into SolidWorks CAD and Fusion360 for fast, accurate modeling.
Conducted impact analysis to optimize design parameters, building a custom testing apparatus using a parallel configuration of strain gauge pads and an Adafruit Metro M4 microcontroller.

Led the prototype manufacturing. Design is modular, chemically inert, completely recyclable or down-cyclable, and highly impact resistant. Hardware is nylon, soft body parts TPU, interior connectors PLA, front door cover polycarbonate, and front lock a neodymium magnet.
Conducted manufacturing feasibility study and plan for quick deployment.

sections.heading: Recognition
sections.content: Our project won first place in Georgia Tech's Mechanical Engineering Summer Capstone Exposition.

gallery.caption: Drop test: the monitor in its case takes a full-height fall onto concrete and keeps running. Surviving the drop is the whole point — a monitor that stops beeping stops being a monitor.
The team at the Georgia Tech Capstone Design Expo, where Keep The Beep took the Mechanical Engineering award.

title: Peace Corps Kenya
description: Served as a STEM Education Teacher in rural Kenya, leading community development projects and teaching Math/Physics.

sections.content: Teaching Math and Physics in Kakamega county secondary school as a Peace Corps Volunteer. My host school mostly comprises students from rural areas and humble backgrounds. A volunteer was requested by the Kakamega host community specifically to aid in teaching; however, I additionally took on side projects with my fellow teachers, students, and other community stakeholders.

sections.heading: Key Contributions
bullets: Prioritized integration into the host community: learned intermediate Swahili and adopted effective methods for classroom management, teaching with extremely limited resources, grant writing, and local lifestyle skills.

Utilized the school's previously untouched projector (when electricity was available) and mobile phones to bring technology literacy and engagement, and led meetings with fellow teachers on technology use.
Started the 'Science and Engineering Club' to encourage critical thinking and practical skill-building with projects like the egg-drop challenge and a DIY anemometer.
Created a 'Climate Smart Kitchen Garden' demonstration plot to encourage improved farming practices and diversified household nutrition, more resilient during increasingly common droughts.

Conducted formal needs analysis with school and community leaders, applied for and received a USAID Small Project Assistance grant, and coordinated construction of a solar well pump, water tower, and distribution pipes serving over 2,000 individuals.

title: EWB-GT: Malawi Project
description: Led the design and implementation of sanitation latrines and handwashing stations for Mpitilira primary school in Malawi.

sections.heading: The Problem
sections.content: Mpitilira primary school in Eastern Malawi lacked sufficient sanitation infrastructure to accommodate the growing school population, and was suffering from disease outbreaks due to open defecation.

sections.heading: The Solution
sections.content: Designed and implemented ventilated double pit latrine blocks for the school alongside handwashing stations to accommodate the existing and future school population. Assessment, designing, construction, and quality control were conducted remotely due to the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic.

sections.heading: Key Contributions
bullets: Completed a fully remote sanitation infrastructure upgrade during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Researched latrine design and iterated features using a decision matrix and community feedback. Multiple alternatives were provided for community input.
Conducted manual structural calculations with additional safety checks given soil pressure and environmental factors.
Used Fusion 360 and AutoCAD for 3D design and dimensioned drawings for use by contractors.

Coordinated with contractors for materials acquisition, construction, and quality control. Under my time, two student latrine blocks (8 toilets) were constructed and the staff latrine block design was finalized.
